name: Lepontic
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Extinct fragmentary Cisalpine Celtic; Glottolog MED is Lejeune 1971 Lepontica (epigraphic wordlist); no stress description found

new_statements.quote: To start with the accentual metrical approach, its fundamental weakness lies in the fact that the stress systems of Ancient Celtic languages are unknown. Only more or less sophisticated hypotheses have been proposed about their nature. In many instances where accentual metrics are involved, the implicit assumption is that the texts have to be scanned with initial dynamic stress. One argument in favour of it is the fact that alliteration, which is particularly suited for stress-initial languages, is of relatively frequent occurrence in Ancient Celtic texts.
new_statements.citation: Stifter, David. 2016. Metrical systems of Celtic traditions. North-Western European Language Evolution (NOWELE) 69(1): 38-94. doi:10.1075/nowele.69.1.02sti
new_statements.locator: p. 59 (section on methodological problems of Ancient Celtic metrics); Lepontic texts discussed pp. 50-52
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is recoverable: the source states outright that the stress system of Lepontic (and the other Ancient Celtic languages) is unknown. The working hypothesis used in metrical scholarship is initial dynamic stress, supported only indirectly by the frequency of alliteration; Stifter applies it to the Lepontic Vergiate and Ornavasso texts ('assuming initial stress', p. 51; 'an accentual scansion with stress on the first syllable', p. 52) but flags it as an assumption.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source's caveat is global (p. 59). For Ornavasso VB·3.1 (p. 52) an initial-stress scansion is shown as compatible with, not evidence for, a quantitative trochaic tetrameter.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about 'Ancient Celtic languages' collectively (Lepontic, Cisalpine Gaulish, Gaulish, Celtiberian), made in a paper on metrics, not a phonological description; evidence base is a corpus of short epigraphic texts, no citation forms. Stifter 2020 (Palaeohispanica 20, §1.4.1 Phonology) and Lexicon Leponticum's Phonology page, the only modern phonological sketches found, are silent on accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Stifter's statement (p. 59) is about the Ancient Celtic languages collectively; the Lepontic-specific applications (pp. 50-52) concern the inscriptions of Vergiate VA·6, Prestino CO·48 (both early Lepontic, pre-400 BCE in the LexLep definition) and Ornavasso VB·3.1 (late phase, 2nd/1st c. BCE, which some classify as Cisalpine Gaulish). Lexicon Leponticum restricts 'Lepontic' to pre-400 BCE texts and treats Cisalpine Gaulish as a separate language (its glottocode not checked here). The catalog entry, if made, should read 'stress system unknown (extinct, epigraphic); initial dynamic stress is the working hypothesis of metrical scholarship', not 'fixed-initial'.

sources.locator: p. 59 (section on methodological problems of Ancient Celtic metrics); Lepontic texts discussed pp. 50-52
sources.note: p. 59: 'the stress systems of Ancient Celtic languages are unknown'; accentual scansions assume initial dynamic stress, alliteration cited as the one argument for it. pp. 50-52 apply this to the Lepontic texts Vergiate VA·6 ('assuming initial stress' gives a trochaic reading), Prestino CO·48, and Ornavasso VB·3.1 ('an accentual scansion with stress on the first syllable' can be superimposed on the quantitative trochaic tetrameter).
Nothing on accent, stress or syncope; bibliography only.
